Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary clinics in Togo predominantly use paper-based patient registers and records at point of care. Aggregated weekly surveillance data (e.g., cases/deaths for 15 diseases) is tallied from facility registries onto paper forms, then sent via SMS using the Argus app on dedicated phones for upward reporting—not patient-level digital entry Argus study. No evidence of routine EMR or DHIS2 at rural clinics; only 11.8% of surveyed doctors nationwide use EMR, reflecting low digitization Doctors EMR survey. Pilots exist: Integrate Health ICBHSS in 21 northern rural facilities focuses on clinical mentoring/supply chains without digital records ICBHSS protocol; DokitaEyes app (230 facilities) for digital patient files, but private/NGO-led, offline-capable, not standard public rural practice; recent World Bank $100M digital project connects facilities to broadband (2024), but focuses on connectivity/skills, not POC systems. National DHIS2 used for aggregate HMIS/IDSR, not facility-level recording. Barriers: poor internet/power in rural areas, low EMR adoption, reliance on paper transmission historically. Policy (e.g., National Digital Health Center) aims at digital transformation, but rural POC remains paper-based, with digital limited to pilots/aggregation. (198 words)

revision_notes: Cited sources (Argus study, ICBHSS protocol, World Bank release) were fetched and support a paper-based baseline, but a fast search surfaced fresher, authoritative evidence of programme-specific digital capture that the original comment omitted: SanteComTogo, a national electronic community health information system, launched March 2024 and has digitised (replacing paper) household registration and care-visit data for over 1,000 community health workers across six districts of the Maritime Region, scaling nationally since. A peer-reviewed 2025 article (Revue Africaine des Sciences Sociales et de la Sante Publique) independently confirms that DHIS2-based digitalisation of health data production has been replacing paper registers since 2021 for malaria chemoprevention and bed-net campaign data. DHIS2's own account of the EPI/immunisation package (since c.2015-2020) also documents decentralisation of data entry to facility level. This constitutes multiple, corroborating, fetched sources for at least partial facility/community-level digital capture, which the original code of 1 (entirely paper) does not reflect. Recalculated to 2 (mostly paper, some digital) rather than higher, as general clinical records and patient registers at most rural clinics remain paper-based and EMR use among doctors nationally is low (~12%).
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare data capture in Togo presents a mixed paper-digital picture rather than a wholly paper-based one. Since 2021, national malaria chemoprevention and bed-net distribution reporting, and since March 2024 the SanteComTogo electronic community health information system, have shifted specific data streams from paper registers to app-based digital capture; SanteComTogo alone covers over 1,000 community health workers across six districts of the Maritime Region at launch, with national scale-up under way. Facility-level immunisation (EPI) data entry via DHIS2 has similarly been decentralised to the facility level for some years. Nonetheless, general patient registration and clinical records at most rural clinics remain paper-based, electronic medical record use among doctors nationally is low (around 12%), and a $100 million World Bank programme approved in December 2024 to connect public institutions to broadband has yet to deliver facility-level point-of-care digital systems. Data capture in rural clinics is therefore best characterised as mostly paper with some digital elements.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Togo's rural policing is handled by Gendarmerie Nationale posts. The Criminal Procedure Code mandates officers (incl. rural gendarmerie) to draft and sign procès-verbaux (PVs) on-site for incidents, with physical custody registers requiring signatures—standard paper-based francophone practice [Togo Code de Procédure Pénale]. UK FCDO arrest guidance describes signed station registers and "police records" for inquiries, implying manual processes [UK Prisoner Pack]. Central WAPIS (2022) enables national data sharing but no evidence of initial rural recording being digital; likely paper first, digitized centrally (scores 1 per rules) [INTERPOL WAPIS]. No rural digital tools on official sites. Score 1: entirely paper-based at rural facilities.

revision_notes: Cited sources were fetched; the Criminal Procedure Code and WAPIS material support the original paper-based assessment, but the UK FCDO prisoner pack is only weakly probative (it describes station registers generically, not specifically rural gendarmerie practice). A search for fresher evidence found that WAPIS/CIPT (operational since 2022) is a central national data-collection and analysis centre in Lomé rather than a rural point-of-capture system, confirming the original view that it does not establish digital recording at rural stations. However, a May 2024 UNDP press release describes a pilot providing computer equipment (14 desktops, printers, scanners) to three rural-region prosecutors' offices (Mandouri/Savanes, Pagouda/Kara, Tabligbo/Maritime) and six police/gendarmerie investigation units, as part of a project to interconnect prosecutors with police judiciaire units. This is suggestive but inconclusive evidence of emerging digitisation reaching rural units, and it is a single source describing a narrow pilot rather than confirmed digital data capture. In line with guidance not to upgrade on a single weak source, the code is kept at 1 (entirely paper), but the row is flagged for human review given this emerging, only partially corroborated evidence.
revised_comments: Rural policing in Togo is conducted mainly through Gendarmerie Nationale posts operating under the Code de Procedure Penale, which requires officers to draft and sign proces-verbaux and maintain physical custody registers on-site, a standard paper-based practice. The West Africa Police Information System (WAPIS), operational since 2022 through Togo's Centre d'Information Policiere in Lome, centralises criminal case data for national and regional sharing but operates at a central rather than rural facility level. A small UNDP-supported pilot in 2024 supplied computer equipment to a handful of rural-region prosecutors' offices and police/gendarmerie investigation units as part of a project to interconnect prosecutors with police judiciaire units, but there is no clear evidence yet that this has changed how case data is captured at the point of contact in rural stations. Data capture at rural police facilities is therefore assessed as entirely paper-based.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Togo's rural registry offices (état civil at prefectures/town halls) predominantly use paper-based recording. Births are declared at local Etat Civil with hospital attestation, recorded in multi-leaflet paper registers; leaflet given as Acte de Naissance. No electronic CRVS database; paper used throughout for transfers to central levels per ECA-APAI report. Low completeness (e.g., 22-30% late registrations via courts). Recent pilots (Dec 2025) allow online requests for copies in 5 communes (some rural like Avé 2), implying scanned paper records for digital access, but core recording at rural facilities remains paper/manual. Pilots indicate emerging digital services, but not at recording stage. Score 2: predominantly paper with some digital pilots.

revision_notes: The original row's Comments text concluded 'Score 2: predominantly paper with some digital pilots' yet the Value Code field recorded 1, an internal inconsistency. The cited sources were fetched and confirm a predominantly paper CRVS system with an emerging digital pilot for requesting copies of civil-status documents in five communes launched December 2025 (Agoe-Nyive 1, Golfe 1, Ave 2, Zio 2, Lacs 1). Further searching found this pilot has continued to develop: a UNDP-supported birth tele-declaration platform has operated in commune Golfe 3 since April 2024, delivering around 14,800 birth certificates in eight months, and in April 2026 the five pilot communes received computer equipment (desktops, printers, scanners) to support the digitisation drive, described by officials as an intermediate step before nationwide rollout. Per the metadata guidance that only facility-level data capture (not higher-level digitisation of already-recorded paper data) should count, the copy-request portal itself is not directly relevant, but the birth tele-declaration platform and the equipping of registry offices for digital processing indicate genuine, if limited, digital capture is beginning to reach rural civil registry offices. Recalculated to 2 (mostly paper, some digital), consistent with the original comment's stated conclusion and resolving the code/comment mismatch.
revised_comments: Civil registration in Togo's rural prefectures and communes remains predominantly paper-based, with births, deaths and marriages recorded in multi-leaflet paper registers at local etat civil offices and low completeness of late registrations (roughly a quarter of cases handled via the courts). Digitisation is nonetheless emerging: since April 2024 a UNDP-supported birth tele-declaration platform has operated in the commune of Golfe 3, delivering around 14,800 birth certificates in its first eight months; since December 2025 an online portal has allowed citizens in five pilot communes (Agoe-Nyive 1, Golfe 1, Ave 2, Zio 2 and Lacs 1) to request copies of civil-status documents and track processing in real time; and in April 2026 these pilot communes received computer equipment to support the digitisation drive, described by officials as an intermediate step ahead of nationwide rollout. This combination of largely paper-based recording with a small but growing set of digital pilots is best characterised as mostly paper with some digital.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Togo's rural primary schools use a hybrid paper-digital system for data collection (attendance, enrollment, grades). Data from 16,000 schools, including rural primaries, is first collected on paper forms at schools, then transmitted to district education inspections for review and subsequent digitization into StatEduc. Digital processing/analysis occurs via DHIS2 EMIS (piloted nationally since 2021 with GPE KIX/Norad support), but initial recording remains paper-based at facility level. No evidence of on-site digital recording in rural schools; digitization is at district level. This aligns with francophone African norms and recent reports (2022-2025). Score 1 as rural facilities record on paper.

revision_notes: All three cited sources were fetched and confirm the original assessment: data from the country's roughly 16,000 pre-primary, primary and secondary schools is first collected on paper forms at school level and only digitised once it reaches district inspectorates, where it is entered into StatEduc and then processed/visualised via a DHIS2-based EMIS operating at national scale since 2019. A further search did not find any evidence of on-site digital data capture in rural primary schools; digitisation consistently occurs only after forms leave the school. The original code of 1 (entirely paper) is confirmed, correcting only the year (previously blank) and minor detail (DHIS2/StatEduc integration dates to 2019 nationally, per DHIS2's own implementation page, rather than 2021 as stated in the original comment, which appears to refer to the GPE KIX-funded EMIS enhancement phase).
revised_comments: Togo's Ministry of Primary, Secondary and Technical Education relies on a hybrid paper-digital education management information system. Data from the country's roughly 16,000 pre-primary, primary and secondary schools is first collected on paper forms at the school level, then forwarded to district education inspectorates for entry into StatEduc, a statistical application used in some twenty countries. Since 2019, StatEduc has been complemented nationally by a DHIS2-based EMIS, developed with GPE KIX and Norad support, which processes and visualises the collected data through dashboards covering enrolment, teacher-pupil ratios and exam results, decentralising analysis to district and school actors. Because data capture at the school itself remains paper-based, with digitisation occurring only once forms reach the district level, rural primary schools are assessed as recording data entirely on paper.
